title: An Introduction to R
text:
Welcome
This book covers getting an answer out of a dataset, and it is written for people who have never programmed. It is the week-one material for SPH5421, Fundamentals of Infectious Disease Modelling, at the NUS Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health.
The outputs on these pages, including the plots, the warnings and the place where R prints NaN instead of a number, were produced by running the code shown directly above them. If a number in the prose disagrees with the number in the output block, the prose is wrong; please report it.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Who this is for
The intended reader is a public health masters student who has used Stata or SPSS through a menu, or who has done their analysis in a spreadsheet and found it difficult to keep track of at a few thousand rows. No programming background is assumed; familiarity with a mean and a median, and a rough idea of what an epidemic curve is, are enough.
By the time you reach the end you should be able to read a CSV into R and form a view about whether to trust it; turn cumulative counts into daily ones without silently losing the first day; find missing values, work out why they are missing, and decide what to do rather than letting R decide for you; group a dataset by month and summarise it; build a figure suitable for a report; and write a small function so that the same calculation done six times is written once. The last chapter asks you to produce a monthly situation report from the raw file, with no scaffolding.
The book also spends time on reading error messages, which is a skill separate from the syntax and is treated as such throughout.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
The data
A single dataset runs through the whole book: Singapore’s 2020 COVID-19 record, 345 daily rows from 22 January to 31 December 2020, with 13 columns. These cover cumulative confirmed cases and deaths, the three Oxford government-response indices, and the six Google Community Mobility series. The record ends with 58,599 confirmed cases and 29 recorded deaths.
It combines three sources: the COVID-19 Data Hub R package (Guidotti & Ardia, 2020), the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker (Hale et al., 2021) and Google’s COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports; Appendix B — The data gives the full citations. For Singapore, the Hub’s figures draw in turn on the Ministry of Health’s daily reporting. Appendix B documents every column, including where it is missing and why. The CSV file itself can be downloaded directly at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro/main/data/sg_covid_data.csv.
It was chosen because it is small enough to inspect in full and because it has the ordinary defects. The death column has 59 leading missing values, and when it does start it starts at 2 rather than at 1, so the obvious way of turning it into daily deaths recovers 27 of the 29. Every mobility column is missing its first 24 days, because Google’s baseline period had not finished when the series begins. The case counts are cumulative, so a plot of the raw column rises monotonically and shows little about when incidence was high. And there is a day in August with 908 cases in a month whose median is 91, which is a reporting artefact rather than a wave. Each of these appears later as a worked example.
The code below is the sort of thing you will be writing by the end of Part IV; none of it needs to make sense yet.

covid <- read_covid()

covid %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(daily_cases = confirmed - lag(confirmed, default = 0)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = daily_cases)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "The shape of Singapore's 2020",
    subtitle = "Peak of 1,426 new cases on 20 April, during the circuit breaker",
    x = NULL,
    y = "New cases"
  )



New confirmed cases per day, computed from the cumulative column in the raw file. The single tall bar in August is the 908-case reporting day, not a second wave.



read_covid() is a shortcut defined in the book’s setup file so that every chapter starts from the same place. The import chapter unwraps it and shows you the read_csv() call inside.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Exercises, hints and solutions
Exercises sit inside the chapters, near the material they exercise. Each states a goal in words and leaves the structure of the answer to you, so deciding how to build the answer is part of the work.
Under most exercises there is a collapsed hint, which names the function or approach to reach for. Under that is a link to the worked solution in Appendix A. The solutions are complete and commented, and each is one click away. Attempting the exercise first is more useful than reading the solution first, but the choice is yours.






SPH5421 students: where to stop



For the live session, work Parts I to IV: everything up to and including Showing it to someone. That is the material the rest of the module builds on.
The whole book takes roughly five and a half hours if you type the code rather than skim it. Parts V and VI, on writing your own functions and the capstone, are for the week after, or for when you meet a problem that needs them. You are not expected to arrive having finished the book.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
How to use this book
Type the code rather than pasting it. Typing makes the structure visible: that aes() sits inside ggplot() rather than next to it, for instance. It also produces your own typos in a setting where the correct version is on the screen above, so you meet the common error messages while their cause is still obvious. There is a copy button on every code block on this site, which is useful when you are re-running something for the fifth time.
Read error messages to the end. R’s errors usually run to two or three lines and the useful line is rarely the first. The tidyverse ones put the diagnosis under a bullet several lines down, along with a suggestion for what to do about it. When you search for a message, paste it in exactly as R printed it, but delete your own object and file names first, since those appear nowhere outside your own session.
Run everything as you read. When a chunk produces something, look at it before scrolling on, then change one thing and run it again: change the 100 to 50, swap mean for median, or remove the na.rm = TRUE and see what changes. Every chunk can be re-run from the top of its chapter, so an experiment that fails costs nothing.
Chapters render in separate R sessions and each one is self-contained, so you can restart R at any point and pick up at the top of a chapter.

title: An Introduction to R
text:
Corrections
Every page has an “Edit this page” link that goes to its source on GitHub, and there is an issue tracker. A wrong number in a teaching resource propagates into every analysis built on it, so corrections are welcome, however small.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.1 R first, then RStudio
This chapter installs two programs, in a particular order, and finishes with a check that they work together. The process takes about twenty minutes, most of which is downloading. If you already have both installed and working, skip to the check at the end of this chapter, run it, and move on.
R is the language and the engine. It is what actually adds the numbers up. RStudio is a front end: an editor, a console, a plot viewer and a file browser stitched together into one window. RStudio does no statistics of its own. When it starts, it goes looking for an R installation on your machine and talks to it.
This is why R goes on first. If you launch RStudio with no R installed, it reports that it cannot find one and refuses to start. Install R, confirm it exists, then install RStudio.
R comes from CRAN, at https://cran.r-project.org. Pick your operating system from the links at the top.
On macOS you will be offered two installers and you have to choose. If your Mac has an Apple silicon chip (M1 and later), take the one whose filename contains arm64. If it is an older Intel Mac, take the x86_64 one. Apple menu, then “About This Mac”, tells you which you have. The wrong choice still runs, under emulation, but more slowly, and it causes trouble later when a package has to be compiled.
On Windows, follow “Download R for Windows”, then “base”, then the big download link. You may see a mention of Rtools on that page. You do not need it for this book. It is for compiling packages from source, which nothing here asks you to do.
On Linux, follow CRAN’s per-distribution instructions. Distribution repositories carry their own r-base package, and it is often several versions behind.
This book needs R 4.1 or newer. Anything from the last few years is fine.
RStudio comes from Posit, at https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/. You want RStudio Desktop, the free open-source version. Posit also sells a paid tier and hosts a server edition, which run on the same editor and add features this book does not use.
Once both are installed, start your work from RStudio rather than from R. R ships with its own minimal window, RGui on Windows and R.app on macOS, which offers a console and little else; RStudio provides the editor, plot viewer and file browser that the rest of this book assumes.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.2 The four panes
RStudio’s window is divided into four, and the first time you see it there is a lot going on. Here is what each one is for.
The Console, bottom left, is R itself. The > prompt is R waiting for you to say something. Type 1 + 1 there and press Enter and you get an answer. Everything that runs in this book runs through this pane, one way or another.
The Source pane, top left, is where your scripts live. It is empty when you first launch, because you have no scripts. Go to File, New File, R Script and it appears, pushing the console down into the lower half. This is where you will spend most of your time.
The Environment pane, top right, lists the objects R currently holds in memory: your data frames, your variables, anything you have created. It is the answer to “did that actually work?”. If you read a CSV and nothing shows up here, the read did not happen. The History tab next to it keeps a log of everything you have typed.
The bottom right pane is a stack of tabs: Files for browsing your folders, Plots for anything you draw, Packages for what is installed, Help for documentation, and Viewer for things like rendered Quarto pages. You will use Plots and Help constantly and largely ignore the rest.
If the layout does not suit you, Tools, Global Options, Pane Layout will rearrange it.
One piece of console behaviour comes up in the first hour, so recognise it now. If the prompt changes from > to +, R has judged your command incomplete and is waiting for the rest of it.
> mean(c(1, 2, 3)
+
+
That happens when you leave a bracket or a quote unclosed. Press Esc: the prompt returns to > and you can start the line again. Pressing Enter instead only adds further + lines, since R is still waiting for the missing closing character.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.3 Three keyboard shortcuts
RStudio has hundreds of keyboard shortcuts and you can see the whole list with Alt+Shift+K on Windows or Option+Shift+K on a Mac. Learn three of them before you write anything.
Run the current line. Ctrl+Enter on Windows and Linux, Cmd+Enter on a Mac. Put your cursor anywhere on a line in your script, press it, and that line is sent to the console and executed. The cursor then drops to the next line, so you can run a script line by line by holding the shortcut down. If you have text selected, it runs the selection instead. This is the shortcut you will use most.
Run the current chunk. Ctrl+Shift+Enter, or Cmd+Shift+Enter. In a Quarto or R Markdown document, code lives in fenced chunks, and this runs the whole chunk your cursor is sitting in. It has no effect in a plain .R script, which has no chunks, and becomes useful once you start writing reports.
Insert the assignment arrow. Alt+-, or Option+-. It types <- with a space either side, which saves three keystrokes on an operator you will type constantly.
R uses <- rather than = for historical and practical reasons. Historically, R inherited the arrow from S, which was written on terminals whose keyboards, borrowed from APL, had a single ← key, so assignment cost one keystroke. The practical reason is that = already has a second job inside function calls, where it names arguments. Compare the two in one line:

x <- mean(c(10, 20, 30), na.rm = TRUE)
x
#> [1] 20

The <- creates an object. The = sets an argument. Keeping them visually distinct lets you read a long function call and see which is which. This book uses <- throughout.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.4 The console and the script
Everything you type in the console runs immediately and is then, for practical purposes, gone. The History tab does keep a record, but it is an undifferentiated stream of everything you tried, wrong attempts and typos included, in the order you happened to type them, which leaves you to reconstruct the analysis from it afterwards.
A script is a file. It runs top to bottom in a fixed order. You can open it in six months, send it to a co-author, put it in a repository, and re-run it to get the same numbers.
Use the console for inspecting the data to see what is in it: nrow(covid), names(covid), checking whether a column is a character or a number. These are questions whose answers you will not need again. Anything you would have to redo, or would need to defend, goes in the script; a line you had to stop and think about is exactly the kind of line to keep in a file.
The awkward case is the analysis that lives entirely in the console. It works until R restarts, at which point the objects are gone and there is no record of how they were made.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.5 Packages, install.packages() and library()

Base R can do a great deal, and it is deliberately conservative about what ships in the box. Most of what you will want lives in a package, and packages come from CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network. CRAN is a network of mirror servers holding many thousands of packages, each of which has passed an automated check on several operating systems before being accepted. That check is the reason install.packages() from a fresh R install usually works without further configuration.
There are two functions involved, and they do different things.
install.packages("tidyverse") downloads the package from CRAN and writes it to your hard disk. You do this once per machine. It takes a while, especially for the tidyverse, because the tidyverse is a meta-package: installing it installs about thirty others.

install.packages("tidyverse")

library(tidyverse) loads an already-installed package into your current R session, so its functions become available by name. You do this every session, at the top of every script. Restart R and it is undone.
The usual analogy is a bookshelf: install.packages() buys the book and puts it on the shelf, while library() takes it down and opens it, which is why the first runs once per machine and the second runs at the top of every session.
The quoting is inconsistent between the two, which is a common source of confusion. install.packages() requires quotes, because it takes the package name as a character string. library() does not, because it evaluates its argument non-standardly and accepts a bare name. Both accept quotes, so quoting in both places is a safe habit if you would rather not remember which is which.
When you run library(tidyverse) in a fresh session, this appears:
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
Your version numbers will differ. The red crosses are not errors. They report that dplyr has a function called filter() and so does base R’s stats package, and that since dplyr was loaded second, typing filter() now calls dplyr’s. That is the version this book uses, and R reports the substitution rather than making it silently. If you need the other one, stats::filter() names it explicitly. The :: means “this function, from that package”.
Read the block when it appears. When a function behaves unexpectedly, masking by a later-loaded package is a common explanation, and the conflicts list is where it was announced.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.6 Getting the data
The book runs on one file, sg_covid_data.csv. It was assembled from three sources: the COVID-19 Data Hub R package (Guidotti & Ardia, 2020), the Oxford COVID-19 Government Response Tracker (Hale et al., 2021) and Google’s COVID-19 Community Mobility Reports; Appendix B gives the full citations. There are two ways to get it.
The thorough way is to take the whole book. Go to https://github.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro, click the green Code button, choose Download ZIP, and unzip it somewhere you will find again, such as your Documents folder rather than Downloads. You now have the data, the source of every chapter, and a .Rproj file. Double-click r-intro.Rproj and RStudio opens with everything pointed at the right place.
The quick way is to take just the CSV, from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CERM-NUS/r-intro/main/data/sg_covid_data.csv. The “Download the data” link in this book’s sidebar points to the same address. Right-click, Save Link As. Then make yourself a folder for this course with a data subfolder inside it, and put the CSV in there:
sph5421/
├── data/
│   └── sg_covid_data.csv
└── analysis.R
Two warnings about that download. Some browsers append .txt to files they treat as plain text, so check that what landed on disk is called sg_covid_data.csv and not sg_covid_data.csv.txt. Second, avoid opening it in Excel to inspect it. Excel offers to save the file back on closing, and saving can rewrite the date column into whatever format your regional settings prefer. To look inside the file, read it into R instead: read_csv() reads the file and does not write to it. The raw file is never edited; every repair to the data happens later, in code. That is what the check below does.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.7 Make the folder a project
With the folder made, turn it into an RStudio project. Go to File, New Project, Existing Directory, browse to the course folder, and click Create Project. RStudio closes and reopens inside the project, and an .Rproj file appears in the folder.
The .Rproj file does three things for you. R now starts with that folder as its working directory, so data/sg_covid_data.csv resolves without a path being typed. The project gets its own R session and its own command history, separate from anything else you have open. And it marks the folder: from now on you open the work by double-clicking the .Rproj file, and everything starts pointed at the right place. If you took the ZIP download in the previous section, you already have a project file, r-intro.Rproj, and can skip these steps.

title: 1  Getting set up
text:
1.8 Does it work?
Open a new script with File, New File, R Script; the green-plus button at the top left of the toolbar does the same thing, as does Ctrl+Shift+N, or Cmd+Shift+N on a Mac. Save it straight away with File, Save, naming it analysis.R — with a project open, the save dialog already starts in the project folder, so the folder ends up matching the tree shown in “Getting the data”. Then type the following in, and run it a line at a time with Ctrl+Enter, or Cmd+Enter on a Mac.

library(tidyverse)

covid <- read_csv("data/sg_covid_data.csv")
#> Rows: 345 Columns: 13
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr   (1): administrative_area_level_1
#> dbl  (11): confirmed, deaths, stringency_index, government_response_index, c...
#> date  (1): date
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 345

You should get 345, and above it a column specification listing 13 columns: one character, eleven numbers and one date. That block is readr reporting what type it assigned to each column. The types are inferred from the first thousand rows, so the block is where a wrong inference can be caught, rather than four steps into an analysis when a column that should be a date turns out to be text.
You will also see the tidyverse startup message from the previous section. It does not appear on this page because the machine that built the book had already loaded the tidyverse before this chapter started, and a package announces itself only the first time a session attaches it.
Now check that graphics work:

ggplot(covid, aes(x = date, y = confirmed)) +
  geom_line()



Cumulative confirmed cases, straight from the raw column. A running total can only go up, so the epidemic is in the slope rather than the height.



A line should appear in the Plots pane, climbing from zero in January to just under sixty thousand by December. Yours will have ggplot2’s default grey background, whereas the figures here do not, because the book applies its own theme to every figure. The data and the geometry are the same.
If the plot does not appear and the Plots pane looks squashed, drag the divider between the panes to make it taller. RStudio cannot draw into a pane a few pixels high.

1.8.1 When it does not work
Three failures account for nearly all of them.
Error in library(tidyverse) : there is no package called ‘tidyverse’
The install did not finish, or finished with an error you scrolled past. Run install.packages("tidyverse") again and watch the output this time. On Windows, if it complains that the package is in use, restart R first.
Error:
! 'data/sg_covid_data.csv' does not exist in current working directory:
  '/Users/you/Desktop'.
R is looking in the wrong place. The message reports the directory it searched, so either the file is not where you think it is, or R’s working directory is not where you think it is. getwd() reports the current working directory:

getwd()
#> [1] "/Users/smishra/Documents/GitHub/r-intro"

Yours will print something else. The fix is a project file rather than a call to setwd(), whose path is specific to one machine and to the current arrangement of its folders. If you skipped “Make the folder a project” above, go back to it now: with a project open, R’s working directory is the project folder, and data/sg_covid_data.csv resolves without a path.
Error: unexpected input in "covid <- read_csv(“"
Something in the line is not valid R. That particular one is a smart quote, the curly “ that Word and Slack substitute for the straight ". R does not recognise it as a quote character at all. If instead you left out a comma you get its sibling:
Error: unexpected symbol in "covid <- read_csv("data/sg_covid_data.csv" nrow"
Both messages quote your line back and stop at the point where the parser failed, so the fault is usually immediately before that point.
If none of those match what you are seeing, copy the error text exactly, with your own file paths and object names removed, and search for it.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.1 Assignment
Type 2 + 2 at the console and R prints 4. Nothing of that calculation is kept, so nothing can be built on it. To work with 345 days of case counts, R has to store values under names, and you have to know what kind of value each name holds.
The second requirement is the one that causes trouble. R will let you put a word into a column of numbers without raising an error: it converts the numbers into text instead, and the mean of the column then comes back as NA. This chapter covers the vocabulary needed to diagnose that quickly.
The Singapore file is used throughout, so load it now. read_covid() is a small helper that ships with this book: it reads data/sg_covid_data.csv and hands back exactly what is in the file, with nothing cleaned and nothing repaired.
Assignment gives a value a name. R’s assignment operator is a left-pointing arrow, made of a < and a -:
first_case <- as.Date("2020-01-23")
first_case
#> [1] "2020-01-23"
Two things happened. R evaluated the right-hand side, and it bound the result to the name first_case. Assignment produces no output; to see the value, type the name on its own line, as above.
That date is the first day this file records a confirmed case. Day one of the file, 22 January, has confirmed equal to zero.
In RStudio, Alt and minus (Option and minus on a Mac) types <- for you. The operator comes up constantly, so learn the shortcut early.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.1.1 Why an arrow and not an equals sign
R inherited <- from S, and S inherited it from APL, whose keyboards had a single key that produced a real ← character. When S moved to keyboards without that key, the arrow was spelled out as two characters and stuck.
= also works for assignment at the top level. This book does not use it, for one reason: inside a function call, = already means something else. In round(x, digits = 2) the digits = 2 tells round() which of its arguments you are filling, and leaves no object called digits behind once the call has finished. Reserving <- for “make an object” and = for “fill an argument” keeps the two distinguishable when you read a line of code.

2.1.2 Naming things
Names may contain letters, numbers, dots and underscores. They cannot start with a number, and they cannot contain spaces or hyphens. daily_cases is fine, daily cases is a syntax error, and daily-cases is read as daily minus cases.
R is case sensitive. Confirmed and confirmed are different objects, and mixing them up produces one of the commonest error messages in R:

covd
#> Error:
#> ! object 'covd' not found

When you see object 'x' not found, R has searched every environment on its search path and found no such name. The usual causes are a typo or a chunk that was never run.
This book uses snake_case: lower case, words joined by underscores. Tidyverse function and argument names follow the same convention, so a script written this way reads consistently from your objects through to the functions you call on them. Within that convention, a useful rule is nouns for data and verbs for functions: an object is named after what it is, so covid and daily_cases describe contents, while a function is named after what it does, so read_covid() and mean() describe actions. A reader who meets either kind of name in the middle of a script can then tell what to expect of it before finding where it was defined.
Some names are best avoided entirely. TRUE and FALSE are reserved and cannot be reassigned, but their abbreviations T and F are ordinary variables. A line such as T <- 0 early in a long script changes the meaning of every later T, so write TRUE and FALSE in full. A second group of names is best left alone because each is already a function: c, data, mean and df all have existing meanings. df in particular is the density function of the F distribution:

df(1, 2, 3)
#> [1] 0.2788548

A data frame named df masks stats::df() on the search path. R can usually tell a function call from a variable and will resolve the reference correctly, but the name now has two meanings on the page, and code that looks df up as a value, such as passing it to another function, gets the data frame rather than the density. Choosing a noun that describes the contents avoids the collision entirely.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.2 R has no scalars
R has no scalar type. What looks like a single number is a vector of length one, and much of R’s behaviour follows from that.

total_deaths <- 29
length(total_deaths)
#> [1] 1
length("Singapore")
#> [1] 1

The vector is the basic unit. c() (for combine) joins values into a longer one:

week_one <- c(0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7)
week_one
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4 5 7
length(week_one)
#> [1] 7

Every column of the Singapore file is a vector of length 345. Pull one out with $:

confirmed <- covid$confirmed
length(confirmed)
#> [1] 345
head(confirmed, 10)
#>  [1]  0  1  3  3  4  5  7  7 10 13

Because the vector is the basic unit, arithmetic works on whole vectors at once. R does not need you to write a loop over 345 days.

head(confirmed * 2, 10)
#>  [1]  0  2  6  6  8 10 14 14 20 26

This is called vectorisation, and it accounts for much of the brevity of R code for data analysis. A column of a table is a vector, so one line of arithmetic applies to all 345 days and the code never has to mention how many days there are. Without it, the same operation requires an explicit loop and an index to manage.
The same idea gives a useful quantity. The confirmed column is cumulative, a running total. The number of new cases on a given day is that day’s total minus the previous day’s. Shift the vector along by one, put a zero on the front so the lengths still match, and subtract:

# new cases are today's running total minus yesterday's, because confirmed is cumulative
previous_day <- c(0, confirmed[-length(confirmed)])
new_cases    <- confirmed - previous_day
head(new_cases, 10)
#>  [1] 0 1 2 0 1 1 2 0 3 3
max(new_cases)
#> [1] 1426
covid$date[which.max(new_cases)]
#> [1] "2020-04-20"

The peak is 1,426 new cases on 20 April 2020, during the dormitory outbreak. The comment above the chunk records why the subtraction is set up this way rather than what each line does; the code shows the what on its own, and a comment that merely repeats it is the first thing to go out of date as the code changes. The result can also be checked: the daily figures sum back to the final cumulative total.

sum(new_cases) == max(confirmed)
#> [1] TRUE

The zero on the front is not an arbitrary filler. The file starts on 22 January with confirmed equal to zero, so 22 January did have zero new cases. Writing that day as missing instead would drop a genuine day from every count made afterwards. dplyr::lag() does the same shift in one call, and lag(confirmed, default = 0) is where that zero goes; the version above is the same idea with the machinery visible.

2.2.1 Subsetting
Square brackets pick elements out by position, counting from 1 rather than 0.

confirmed[1]
#> [1] 0
confirmed[1:5]
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4
confirmed[length(confirmed)]
#> [1] 58599

A negative index means everything except, which is what confirmed[-length(confirmed)] did above: all of it bar the last day.
You can also subset with a logical vector, keeping the elements marked TRUE:

covid$date[new_cases > 1000]
#> [1] "2020-04-20" "2020-04-21" "2020-04-22" "2020-04-23"

Four days in 2020 had more than a thousand new cases, and they run consecutively from 20 April. dplyr::filter() expresses the same operation more readably on a table, and underneath it does what this line does: build a logical vector, then retain the elements it marked TRUE.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.3 Vector types and missing values
Every vector has a type, and every element of a vector has the same type. Four types matter for data work:

typeof(TRUE)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(2L)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(29)
#> [1] "double"
typeof("Singapore")
#> [1] "character"

The four types are logical, integer, double and character. (Two more exist, complex and raw, which are not needed for the material in this book.)
Integer and double are both numbers, and R makes the distinction awkwardly. A number you type is a double unless you stick an L on the end. A colon range is an integer.

typeof(1:5)
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(5 / 2)
#> [1] "double"
identical(1, 1L)
#> [1] FALSE
1 == 1L
#> [1] TRUE

identical() reports that they are different objects; == reports that they hold the same value. Both are correct, and the distinction rarely matters in practice. What does matter is that doubles are stored in binary floating point, which cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly:

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
#> [1] FALSE
0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3
#> [1] 5.551115e-17

This is not specific to R. Any language using IEEE 754 doubles behaves the same way, including spreadsheet software. Testing two calculated numbers with == is therefore unreliable; use near(), which allows a small tolerance:

near(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)
#> [1] TRUE

Logical values are TRUE and FALSE, and R treats them as 1 and 0 in arithmetic. A count of how many elements satisfy a condition is therefore sum() of the logical vector, and the proportion is mean() of it:

sum(covid$confirmed > 10000)
#> [1] 254
mean(covid$stringency_index > 50)
#> [1] 0.5681159

The count is 254 days of 2020 with more than ten thousand cumulative cases, and the stringency index was above 50 on 57% of days.

2.3.1 NA
NA is R’s marker for a value that should exist but is not recorded. It is not zero, not an empty string, and not a statement that the data are complete. Almost any operation involving an NA returns NA, because the result of that operation is unknown too.

NA + 1
#> [1] NA
mean(c(1, 2, NA))
#> [1] NA

The propagation is deliberate: if one of three numbers is unknown, their mean is unknown as well, so R returns NA rather than averaging the two values it has.
The deaths column in this file makes it concrete. Singapore recorded no COVID-19 deaths for the first two months of the epidemic, and this file records those days as missing rather than as zero.

head(covid$deaths, 12)
#>  [1] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
sum(is.na(covid$deaths))
#> [1] 59
mean(covid$deaths)
#> [1] NA

There are 59 missing days, and so the mean of the column is NA. To get an answer you have to say explicitly that you are willing to ignore the gaps:

mean(covid$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 23.75874

Whether that is the right thing to do is a question about the deaths data, not about R. na.rm = TRUE drops the 59 unrecorded days and averages the 286 that remain, so the number returned is the mean of the days the source reported, which is not the mean of 2020. Which of the two you want depends on the question being asked, and the default behaviour at least requires the choice to be made explicitly.
Two more properties of NA come up in daily work. Testing it with == does not work, because “an unknown value” is not equal to anything, including another unknown value:

NA == NA
#> [1] NA

Use is.na() instead:

is.na(c(1, NA, 3))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE

NA also comes in typed forms. Bare NA is logical; there are also NA_integer_, NA_real_ and NA_character_, so that a missing value can sit inside a vector without changing its type. You rarely type these yourself, but you will see them in error messages.

typeof(NA)
#> [1] "logical"
typeof(NA_character_)
#> [1] "character"
typeof(c(NA, 1))
#> [1] "double"

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
section: 2.4 Coercion, or how a column of numbers becomes text
text:
2.4 Coercion, or how a column of numbers becomes text
A vector holds one type, so combining two types forces R to choose one of them.

c(1, "a")
#> [1] "1" "a"

R issued no error or warning; it converted the number 1 into the string "1", because that is the only way to hold both values in one vector. The rule runs one way only, from least to most flexible: logical values can be represented as integers, integers as doubles, and doubles as character strings, so a combination takes the type furthest along that sequence.

typeof(c(TRUE, 1L))
#> [1] "integer"
typeof(c(1L, 2.5))
#> [1] "double"
typeof(c(2.5, "Singapore"))
#> [1] "character"

Nothing here is a bug, and no warning is issued at any step, which is why the conversion is easy to miss. Consider a spreadsheet of daily deaths in which one cell reads "not reported" instead of being left blank. That single cell turns the entire column to character on import, and then:

mean(c("1", "a"))
#> Warning in mean.default(c("1", "a")): argument is not numeric or logical:
#> returning NA
#> [1] NA

The warning is the useful part: argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA. When you see it, you have a character column that you thought was numeric. typeof() on the column confirms it in one line.
Going the other way is explicit, and R does warn:

as.numeric(c("1", "a"))
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
#> [1]  1 NA

NAs introduced by coercion means R turned a value into NA because it could not parse it. Sometimes that is what you intended; sometimes it has removed a large part of the column. Count the missing values afterwards with sum(is.na(x)) to find out which.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.5 Recycling
When two vectors in an arithmetic expression have different lengths, R repeats the shorter one until it is long enough. You have already relied on this: in confirmed * 2, the 2 is a vector of length one and it got recycled 345 times.
That is the useful case. Recycling also applies when neither vector has length one, which is where it causes trouble.






Predict before you run



c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) produces a vector of length four. Write down the four numbers you expect, and whether you expect a warning. Then run it.



c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)
#> [1] 11 22 13 24

No warning was issued here: four is a multiple of two, so R recycled the shorter vector twice and reported nothing. Change the length to three and a warning appears:

c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)
#> Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20): longer object length is not a multiple of
#> shorter object length
#> [1] 11 22 13

longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length reports that the two vectors do not line up. The mechanism is the same in both cases; the warning appears only when the lengths are not multiples, not when the recycling is unintended. Checking length() on vectors before combining them is the reliable way to catch this.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.6 Calling functions
A function has a name, takes arguments in brackets, and gives back a value. mean(new_cases) takes one argument and returns one number. Functions nest, and R works from the inside out:

round(mean(new_cases), 2)
#> [1] 169.85
median(new_cases)
#> [1] 40

A mean of 169.85 new cases a day against a median of 40 indicates a strongly right-skewed distribution, which matches the epidemic: most of 2020 had low daily counts, and a few weeks in April and May had very high ones.
Arguments can be given by position or by name. These three calls are identical:

seq(1, 10, 3)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10
seq(from = 1, to = 10, by = 3)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10
seq(by = 3, to = 10, from = 1)
#> [1]  1  4  7 10

Position only works if you remember the order. Names work regardless of order, and they record in the call itself which argument is being set. Pass the first argument or two positionally, since mean(new_cases) is unambiguous, and name everything after that.
Most arguments have defaults, so you only supply the ones you want to change. args() shows you what they are:

args(round)
#> function (x, digits = 0, ...) 
#> NULL
args(mean)
#> function (x, ...) 
#> NULL

round(x, digits = 0) means that if you do not say otherwise, you get whole numbers. mean(x, ...) is less helpful, because mean is generic and the real arguments live in the method; this is one of the places where R’s help page tells you more than the code does.
round() has one behaviour to watch for:

round(0.5)
#> [1] 0
round(1.5)
#> [1] 2
round(2.5)
#> [1] 2

round(0.5) is 0 and round(1.5) is 2. R rounds halves to the nearest even number rather than upward, following the IEC 60559 standard, so that rounding a long column of values does not accumulate an upward bias. ?round documents this. The behaviour is intended, and it can still surprise someone checking totals by hand.

2.6.1 Reading a help page
Every function in R ships with documentation. A question mark opens it:

?mean
help("mean")

If you do not know the name, two question marks searches the text of every installed help page:

??"standard deviation"

Help pages have a fixed structure, and reading them from top to bottom is rarely the quickest route. A more efficient order begins with the Usage section, which shows the function signature with every default filled in, so you can see what may be passed. From there, read only the two or three entries in Arguments that are relevant to the call you are writing. The Examples at the bottom of the page are runnable, and example(mean) runs them without opening the page; they are often the fastest way to see the function used correctly. The Details section matters most when something has already gone wrong, since that is where behaviour such as the rounding rule above is described, and the Value section settles what type the function returns, which is more often useful than it first appears.
Tidyverse functions carry the same documentation, typeset more legibly at https://tidyverse.org. Base R help pages are frequently terse, and much of that documentation was written for specialists rather than beginners. Searching for the function name plus “r” will usually find explanations in more ordinary language.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.7 Packages and where functions live
R ships with a few thousand functions. Everything else lives in packages: bundles of functions, documentation and sometimes data, written by other people and published on CRAN.
Installing is a one-off, per machine. It downloads and compiles code onto your hard disk.

install.packages("tidyverse")

Loading is per session. It takes an installed package and makes its functions available by name.

library(tidyverse)

The distinction matters in practice. install.packages() belongs at the console, typed by hand, and not in a script; running it on every render costs minutes and requires an internet connection. library() belongs at the top of every script, because a script that does not load the packages it uses will fail on any machine where those packages are not already attached. The quotation marks are required by one and not the other, which is an inconsistency in R rather than a mistake on your part.

2.7.1 The masking message
library(tidyverse) prints a block of text when it loads. Read it.
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
Loading dplyr on its own reports the same thing in more detail:
Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
Nothing has broken, and the mechanism behind the message is the search path: R keeps an ordered list of the places it looks for a name.

head(search(), 15)
#>  [1] ".GlobalEnv"        "package:scales"    "package:patchwork"
#>  [4] "package:here"      "package:lubridate" "package:forcats"  
#>  [7] "package:stringr"   "package:dplyr"     "package:purrr"    
#> [10] "package:readr"     "package:tidyr"     "package:tibble"   
#> [13] "package:ggplot2"   "package:tidyverse" "package:stats"

When you type filter(...), R walks that list from left to right and uses the first filter it finds. Every package you attach is inserted near the front, so a newly loaded package wins against anything loaded before it. package:dplyr sits ahead of package:stats, so filter means dplyr’s.
stats::filter has not been deleted, and you can still reach it by giving its full address. The double colon means “the function called filter from the package called stats, regardless of the search path”:

head(round(stats::filter(covid$confirmed, rep(1/7, 7)), 1), 10)
#>  [1]   NA   NA   NA  3.3  4.3  5.6  7.0  8.9 10.9 12.7

That is a seven-day moving average of the cumulative curve, which is the job stats::filter() does. It returns a time series object, hence the header lines about start, end and frequency, and the first three values are NA because a seven-day window cannot be centred on day one. None of this has anything to do with selecting rows from a table:

dplyr::filter(covid, stringency_index > 80)$date
#> [1] "2020-04-10" "2020-04-25" "2020-05-01"

Two functions share a name and do unrelated jobs. The conflicts message exists so that the collision is visible when the package is attached, rather than later when a result looks wrong.
The same applies to lag(). dplyr::lag() shifts a vector along by one position, which is exactly what you did by hand earlier. stats::lag() shifts a time series’ index and leaves the values alone. If you ever compute daily cases and get a column of zeroes, this is why.
This is also why library() goes at the top of a script. If dplyr has not been loaded and you call filter() on a data frame, the call reaches stats::filter, and the resulting error does not point at the missing library() line.
Error: object 'confirmed' not found
stats::filter() has no idea that confirmed is a column of the thing you handed it, so it tries to find an object by that name and fails. The fix is a library(dplyr) or library(tidyverse) line you left out, and the error message does not say so.
Writing dplyr::filter() in full removes the ambiguity, at the cost of a package prefix on every call. It earns that cost in code you distribute, where the reader may have a different set of packages attached. For everyday analysis, load the package and read the conflicts message; if you would prefer collisions to raise an error instead of being resolved by precedence, the conflicted package does that.

title: 2  Objects, vectors and functions
text:
2.8 Exercise

Exercise 2.1 (Build a week by hand) The first seven cumulative confirmed counts in the file are 0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5 and 7.

Store them in a vector called week_one and confirm that R agrees it has seven elements and holds doubles.
Work out how many new cases were recorded on each of days two to seven, using only subsetting and subtraction.
Add the label "week one" to the front of week_one, look at the type again, and then try to multiply the result by two. Explain in one sentence what R did to your numbers and why the arithmetic now fails.
Make a copy of week_one with the fourth element replaced by NA, then find its mean twice, once as R gives it to you and once telling mean() to drop the missing value.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 2, two vectors of the same length subtract element by element, so you need one vector holding days two to seven and another holding days one to six. For part 3, look at typeof() before and after.



Worked solution

title: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
3.1 Three vectors and a problem
A data frame holds several variables of different types in one object, with the same number of rows in each. That constraint is what allows a dataset to be filtered, sorted and summarised without keeping track by hand of which value belongs with which. This chapter covers what a data frame is made of, what a tibble changes, and what tidy data means.
Take three days of the Singapore record, in the week the circuit breaker began, and store each variable in its own vector.
day        <- as.Date(c("2020-04-06", "2020-04-07", "2020-04-08"))
confirmed  <- c(1375, 1481, 1623)
stringency <- c(45.37, 62.04, 76.85)
The values themselves are all present, but the correspondence between the three vectors is not recorded anywhere: that the second element of each refers to the same day is an assumption you are holding, not something R knows or enforces.
Sorting one of them shows the consequence. Sort the stringency values from highest to lowest, which is a reasonable thing to want:
sort(stringency, decreasing = TRUE)
#> [1] 76.85 62.04 45.37
day
#> [1] "2020-04-06" "2020-04-07" "2020-04-08"
stringency has been reordered and day has not, so if that sorted vector is assigned back over the old one, the 7 April stringency score now sits alongside 6 April, and nothing in the session records that the two vectors have come apart. There is no error and no warning, and a plot drawn from them still looks plausible.
With 345 rows and 13 variables, maintaining that correspondence by hand is not workable, which is what data frames are for.
crumbs: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
section: 3.2 A data frame is a list of columns
text:
3.2 A data frame is a list of columns
data.frame() binds vectors together so that they can only be manipulated as a unit.

three_days <- data.frame(day, confirmed, stringency)
three_days
#>          day confirmed stringency
#> 1 2020-04-06      1375      45.37
#> 2 2020-04-07      1481      62.04
#> 3 2020-04-08      1623      76.85

Now sorting means sorting rows, and the rows carry their contents with them:

three_days[order(three_days$stringency, decreasing = TRUE), ]
#>          day confirmed stringency
#> 3 2020-04-08      1623      76.85
#> 2 2020-04-07      1481      62.04
#> 1 2020-04-06      1375      45.37

The row numbers on the left have gone 3, 2, 1. Each row moved as a piece.
Underneath, a data frame is a list of vectors, which becomes visible if you strip the class off it:

unclass(three_days)
#> $day
#> [1] "2020-04-06" "2020-04-07" "2020-04-08"
#> 
#> $confirmed
#> [1] 1375 1481 1623
#> 
#> $stringency
#> [1] 45.37 62.04 76.85
#> 
#> attr(,"row.names")
#> [1] 1 2 3

The output is a named list of three vectors plus an attribute recording the row names, and that is all a data frame contains. Everything else, the printing, nrow(), the two-dimensional subsetting, is behaviour attached to that list by its class. R will confirm the underlying structure if asked directly:

is.list(three_days)
#> [1] TRUE
length(three_days)
#> [1] 3
lengths(three_days)
#>        day  confirmed stringency 
#>          3          3          3

length() on a data frame counts the elements of the underlying list, which is the number of columns. lengths(), with the s, gives the length of each element, which is the number of rows repeated once per column. nrow() and ncol() are friendlier names for the same two facts.
Two properties follow directly from the list-of-vectors implementation.
Columns may be of different types. A list can hold anything, so one element can be a Date vector, the next a double vector, the next a character vector. Each column is internally uniform, which is the vector rule from Section 2.3, but columns need not agree with each other. That is what makes a data frame a suitable shape for a dataset, where dates, counts and labels sit side by side. A matrix cannot do this; every cell of a matrix has one type.

sapply(three_days, class)
#>        day  confirmed stringency 
#>     "Date"  "numeric"  "numeric"

Rows must line up. The list is not free to hold vectors of any length, because the rectangle would stop being a rectangle. Give data.frame() mismatched lengths and it refuses:

data.frame(day = 1:3, phase = c("pre", "circuit breaker"))
#> Error in `data.frame()`:
#> ! arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 2

arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 2 is a useful error: it arrives at the moment the mistake is made rather than several steps later.
Every operation on a rectangle, filtering rows, creating columns, grouping and summarising, relies on row i of every column referring to the same observation. filter() can drop 200 rows without any separate check that the variables stayed aligned, because misalignment is not representable.

3.2.1 Recycling in data.frame()

There is one exception to that constraint, and it is a long-standing one. If the short vector’s length divides the long one exactly, data.frame() recycles instead of raising an error:

data.frame(day = 1:6, phase = c("pre", "circuit breaker"))
#>   day           phase
#> 1   1             pre
#> 2   2 circuit breaker
#> 3   3             pre
#> 4   4 circuit breaker
#> 5   5             pre
#> 6   6 circuit breaker

The result is six rows with alternating labels, produced without a warning. This is the recycling rule from Section 2.5 applied to column construction. It is convenient when intended and silent when not, so a mistyped or mis-subsetted vector can produce a table that looks complete.
crumbs: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles

title: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
3.3 Tibbles
A tibble is a data frame with several of its older behaviours changed. read_csv() returns one, so this is what covid has been all along:

class(covid)
#> [1] "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df"      "tbl"         "data.frame"

Reading the class vector from the right, the object is a data.frame, so anything that accepts a data frame accepts it. tbl and tbl_df are the tibble classes, which change how it prints and how it is subsetted. spec_tbl_df is readr’s marker, carrying the column specification it worked out while reading the file: which column it took to be a date, which it took to be numbers, which it left as text.
The differences that matter in practice are the following.

3.3.1 Printing reports types and dimensions

covid
#> # A tibble: 345 × 13
#>    administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths date       stringency_index
#>    <chr>                           <dbl>  <dbl> <date>                <dbl>
#>  1 Singapore                           0     NA 2020-01-22             19.4
#>  2 Singapore                           1     NA 2020-01-23             25  
#>  3 Singapore                           3     NA 2020-01-24             25  
#>  4 Singapore                           3     NA 2020-01-25             25  
#>  5 Singapore                           4     NA 2020-01-26             25  
#>  6 Singapore                           5     NA 2020-01-27             25  
#>  7 Singapore                           7     NA 2020-01-28             25  
#>  8 Singapore                           7     NA 2020-01-29             25  
#>  9 Singapore                          10     NA 2020-01-30             25  
#> 10 Singapore                          13     NA 2020-01-31             25  
#> # ℹ 335 more rows
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: government_response_index <dbl>,
#> #   containment_health_index <dbl>,
#> #   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   parks_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>,
#> #   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl>, …

The printout shows ten rows, then a count of what was left out, then the names and types of the columns too wide to show. Read the <chr>, <dbl> and <date> labels under the column names: a column that is character when you assumed it was numeric is a frequent source of confusion, and the tibble reports the type before any analysis is written.
An old-style data frame does not do this. Print the same 345 rows as a data.frame and R sends all of them to the console without type labels, so the header scrolls off the screen. Do it once to see what it looks like, then use head():

head(as.data.frame(covid)[, 1:5])
#>   administrative_area_level_1 confirmed deaths       date stringency_index
#> 1                   Singapore         0     NA 2020-01-22            19.44
#> 2                   Singapore         1     NA 2020-01-23            25.00
#> 3                   Singapore         3     NA 2020-01-24            25.00
#> 4                   Singapore         3     NA 2020-01-25            25.00
#> 5                   Singapore         4     NA 2020-01-26            25.00
#> 6                   Singapore         5     NA 2020-01-27            25.00


3.3.2 No accidental factors
Before R 4.0.0, released in April 2020, data.frame() and read.csv() converted every character column into a factor by default, because the stringsAsFactors argument defaulted to TRUE. A factor stores its values as integer codes against a table of levels, which is appropriate for a categorical variable in a model and not for a column of free text or identifiers.
The behaviour is still available on request, and it has one consequence that is easy to overlook:

phase <- data.frame(label = c("pre", "circuit breaker"), stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
phase$label
#> [1] pre             circuit breaker
#> Levels: circuit breaker pre

Levels: circuit breaker pre is alphabetical, so “circuit breaker” sorts before “pre” and any plot will show them in that order. R 4.0.0 changed the default to FALSE, one of the few backwards-incompatible changes the language has made. Tibbles never performed the conversion.
Factors are useful when requested deliberately. A severity label that should read low, medium, high rather than alphabetically is a case for factor(), because you name the levels in the order you want and everything downstream uses that order. The difference is that the conversion is then explicit in the code.

3.3.3 Subsetting stays a data frame
Single-bracket subsetting of one column behaves differently in the two classes.






Predict before you run



old below is the same data as covid, converted to an old-style data frame. Both of the next two expressions ask for one column with a single pair of square brackets. Decide, before running them, whether each returns a rectangle of 345 rows and 1 column, or a bare vector of 345 numbers.



old <- as.data.frame(covid)
class(old[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "numeric"
class(covid[, "confirmed"])
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

The data frame dropped a dimension and returned a vector, whereas the tibble returned a one-column table.

covid[, "confirmed"]
#> # A tibble: 345 × 1
#>    confirmed
#>        <dbl>
#>  1         0
#>  2         1
#>  3         3
#>  4         3
#>  5         4
#>  6         5
#>  7         7
#>  8         7
#>  9        10
#> 10        13
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

The old behaviour comes from [.data.frame having a drop argument that defaults to TRUE: ask for a single column and R returns its contents rather than a one-column table. That is convenient interactively and a problem inside a pipeline, because a function two steps downstream that expected a data frame receives a numeric vector and fails with a message about something else entirely. Tibbles set drop = FALSE, so [ always returns a tibble.
When you do want the bare vector, say so with $ or double brackets, both of which mean “give me the contents of this element” and work identically on both kinds of rectangle:

class(covid$confirmed)
#> [1] "numeric"
class(covid[["confirmed"]])
#> [1] "numeric"


3.3.4 No silent partial matching
$ on an old-style data frame will complete a partial column name for you:

head(old$conf, 5)
#> [1] 0 1 3 3 4

There is no column called conf. R found confirmed, took it as the intended match, and returned it without comment. If the file also had a confirmed_cases_dormitory column the match would be ambiguous and $ would return NULL, so the same line would behave differently on a file that differs only in having an extra column.
Tibbles warn:

head(covid$conf, 5)
#> Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `conf`.
#> NULL

The result is a warning saying the column is unknown or uninitialised, followed by NULL. The same warning appears for an ordinary typo, so covid$confrimed is reported rather than silently returning NULL into a calculation.

3.3.5 Choosing between them
Use tibbles for anything you write. When an older package rejects one, and a few statistical packages still do, convert at the point of the call:

class(as.data.frame(covid))
#> [1] "data.frame"

as_tibble() converts back. The two are interconvertible, so the choice is local to the call rather than a commitment for the whole project.

title: 3  Rectangles: data frames and tibbles
text:
3.4 Tidy data
Tidy data is a rule about what goes into which part of the rectangle, and it has three clauses:

Each variable is a column.
Each observation is a row.
Each value is a cell.

The three clauses are easy to state, but real spreadsheets violate them routinely: twelve columns named January to December, a column holding both a measurement and its unit, or two rows per patient because before and after were recorded side by side.
Tidyverse functions assume tidy input. Once the data are in that shape, filter(), mutate(), group_by() and ggplot() all work without further reshaping.
Applying the definition to this file means first establishing what one observation is:

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 345
length(unique(covid$date))
#> [1] 345
length(unique(covid$administrative_area_level_1))
#> [1] 1

The output shows 345 rows, 345 distinct dates and one country, so the unit of observation is a country-day; since the country never varies, in practice it is a day. Each column is a variable measured on that day: a cumulative case count, a cumulative death count, a policy index, six mobility series. There is one row per observation, one column per variable and one value per cell, so this file arrives tidy, which is convenient for the book; data you are handed elsewhere often will not be.

3.4.1 A column that says nothing
administrative_area_level_1 deserves a second look:

table(covid$administrative_area_level_1)
#> 
#> Singapore 
#>       345

The column has one distinct value across all 345 rows. A column that never varies cannot explain, predict, group or distinguish anything. It is present because this extract was taken from a multi-country archive in which the column did vary, and selecting a single country left the label behind.
Counting distinct values in every column is a habit to build on any new dataset, because both ends of the result tell you something. A column with one distinct value carries no information. A column with as many distinct values as there are rows is an identifier rather than a measurement, which is what date is here. Anything in between is a variable you can actually work with.

sapply(covid, function(column) length(unique(column)))
#>                        administrative_area_level_1 
#>                                                  1 
#>                                          confirmed 
#>                                                333 
#>                                             deaths 
#>                                                 27 
#>                                               date 
#>                                                345 
#>                                   stringency_index 
#>                                                 13 
#>                          government_response_index 
#>                                                 23 
#>                           containment_health_index 
#>                                                 21 
#> retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 50 
#>  grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 53 
#>                 parks_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 76 
#>      transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 61 
#>            workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 74 
#>           residential_percent_change_from_baseline 
#>                                                 47

The function(column) argument is an anonymous function, defined at the point of use rather than given a name.
stringency_index takes 13 distinct values over the year, which reflects how it is constructed: it is a score assembled from a handful of policy indicators, so it changes only when one of those indicators changes. The series therefore moves in steps, and each step marks a discrete policy change.

3.4.2 When the file is not tidy
Untidy files are common. The usual shapes are a header row of dates or months, one column containing two variables combined, and observations split across several rows. tidyr provides pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() for reshaping between wide and long layouts. This book does not devote a chapter to reshaping, because the Singapore file does not require it, and the operations are easier to follow once the material here is familiar.

text:
3.5 Exercise

Exercise 3.1 (Take a tibble apart) Using covid as loaded at the top of this chapter:

Show, with code rather than assertion, that covid is a list, how many elements that list has, and that every element has the same length. Say in one sentence which of those two numbers is the number of rows and which is the number of columns.
Find out the type of every column without printing the whole tibble.
Build a small tibble by hand recording three dates in Singapore’s 2020 policy timeline, 7 April, 2 June and 19 June, alongside a short label for each. Give the columns snake_case names that say what each column holds. Then explain in two sentences why holding those as a tibble is safer than holding the dates and the labels as two separate vectors.
Convert covid to an old-style data frame and find one behaviour, other than printing, that differs from the tibble. Show it.








Stuck? Open for a hint (not the answer)





For part 1, three functions from this chapter do the whole job: one asks whether it is a list, one counts the elements, one measures each element. For part 2, sapply() applies a function to every column and collects the answers into one named vector.



Worked solution

title: 4  Reading the epidemic in
text:
4.1 Where the file is
Everything in this book runs on one file: sg_covid_data.csv, 345 rows covering 22 January to 31 December 2020, one row per day. Up to now read_covid() has been supplying it. This chapter covers what that function does and what happens at import more generally.
Import is a common source of errors, and most of them are silent. A date column that arrives as text makes the time series plot in alphabetical order; a missing value coded as -99 that arrives as a number makes the mean wrong; a leading zero disappears from a postcode. None of these raises an error. Most are caught by reading the messages R prints at import time, which is why this book leaves those messages switched on.
R has a working directory: the folder it treats as “here” when you hand it a relative path. It can be set from inside a script, with a line such as setwd("/Users/swapnil/Documents/GitHub/r-intro"). That path is specific to one machine, so the script fails for a colleague, after the folder is moved, or on a teaching-lab computer.
here::here() avoids the problem. The here package looks upward from wherever R happens to be until it finds the top of the project, identified by an .Rproj file, a .git directory or a _quarto.yml, and builds paths from there.
here()
#> [1] "/Users/smishra/Documents/GitHub/r-intro"
That is this project’s root on the machine that rendered this page; on another machine here() returns that machine’s project root, so paths built from it resolve to the same files. Naming the folders as separate arguments lets it assemble a path with the correct separator for Windows, macOS or Linux.
here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv")
#> [1] "/Users/smishra/Documents/GitHub/r-intro/data/sg_covid_data.csv"
Writing here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv") costs a few extra characters and leaves the script working on any machine where the project has been cloned, whatever directory R was started from. Treat this as the permanent habit: no setwd() and no absolute paths, in every script.

title: 4  Reading the epidemic in
text:
4.2 read_csv()

readr’s read_csv() takes a path and returns a tibble.

covid <- read_csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))
#> Rows: 345 Columns: 13
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr   (1): administrative_area_level_1
#> dbl  (11): confirmed, deaths, stringency_index, government_response_index, c...
#> date  (1): date
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

The object is named after what it holds: covid, not df or data — the latter masks a base R function. The file itself is read-only: the CSV in data/ is never edited, and every repair happens in code.
The output above is a message rather than an error; read each line of it.
Rows: 345 Columns: 13. Check this against what you expect before you do anything else. If you were told the file covers a year of daily data and R reports 345 rows, that is 2020 from 22 January onward, and it adds up. If R had said 344, you would want to know which day went missing and why.
Delimiter: ",". readr worked out the separator by looking at the first few lines. Files exported from European locales often use a semicolon, because the comma serves as the decimal mark there; read_csv2() handles those.
chr (1), dbl (11), date (1). These are the guessed column types. Three points matter here.
date came in as a real Date, not as text. readr recognises the ISO 8601 form YYYY-MM-DD and parses it. Because of that, you can subtract one date from another, sort chronologically, and pass dates directly to ggplot().
Every count is dbl, not integer. readr’s guesser does not distinguish whole numbers from decimals; anything numeric arrives as a double. Nothing goes wrong as a result, but it explains why confirmed is <dbl> when it counts people.
One column is chr. That is administrative_area_level_1, the constant “Singapore” you met in Section 3.4.
The two lines at the bottom are hints rather than warnings. spec() prints the full specification, one line per column, which is what to use when the summary is truncated with a ...:

spec(covid)
#> cols(
#>   administrative_area_level_1 = col_character(),
#>   confirmed = col_double(),
#>   deaths = col_double(),
#>   date = col_date(format = ""),
#>   stringency_index = col_double(),
#>   government_response_index = col_double(),
#>   containment_health_index = col_double(),
#>   retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   parks_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double(),
#>   residential_percent_change_from_baseline = col_double()
#> )

The empty format = "" on date means readr used its own ISO guesser rather than a format you supplied. The other hint offers show_col_types = FALSE to silence the message. That is reasonable once you have read the message and stated the types explicitly, as in Section 4.4; before then the message is the only report you get on how the file was parsed.

4.2.1 The dates readr cannot guess
readr guesses dates only for the ISO form. Any other layout is read as character, without a warning, because text is a valid column type and there is nothing for readr to object to.

read_csv(I("date,cases\n07/04/2020,106\n08/04/2020,142\n"))
#> Rows: 2 Columns: 2
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr (1): date
#> dbl (1): cases
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   date       cases
#>   <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 07/04/2020   106
#> 2 08/04/2020   142

The column comes in as <chr>. 07/04/2020 is 7 April under day-first conventions and 4 July under month-first ones, and only knowledge of the source can settle which was meant. State the format explicitly, using the same %d, %m, %Y codes that strptime() uses:

read_csv(
  I("date,cases\n07/04/2020,106\n08/04/2020,142\n"),
  col_types = cols(
    date  = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
    cases = col_double()
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   date       cases
#>   <date>     <dbl>
#> 1 2020-04-07   106
#> 2 2020-04-08   142


4.2.2 Missing values that are not blank
read_csv() treats an empty cell and the literal string NA as missing, but health data often use other codes. If your file codes missing as -99, ., N/A or Not reported, say so, or those values will be read as data:

read_csv(
  here("data", "some_other_file.csv"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A", "Not reported")
)

With a numeric sentinel such as -99, nothing will appear to be wrong. The minimum will be -99 and the mean will be pulled downward, yet every graph will still render. Checking the minimum and maximum of each numeric column after import will usually reveal a sentinel of this kind.

title: 4  Reading the epidemic in
text:
4.3 read.csv() and read_csv()

Base R has its own reader, read.csv(), spelled with a dot rather than an underscore. It returns a data frame rather than a tibble, it prints no column specification, and it does not parse dates, so the date column arrives as character. The two names differ by one character and are easy to type interchangeably by mistake.

old <- read.csv(here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"))
class(old)
#> [1] "data.frame"
class(old$date)
#> [1] "character"
head(old$date, 3)
#> [1] "2020-01-22" "2020-01-23" "2020-01-24"

All three differences are visible above: no column specification is printed, class() reports a plain data.frame, and date holds strings that look like dates. The name old is itself a weak one, used here only for contrast: it records how the object was read rather than what it holds. Arithmetic on that column fails:

old$date - old$date[1]
#> Error in `old$date - old$date[1]`:
#> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator

non-numeric argument to binary operator reports that the subtraction was attempted on text. The repair is an explicit conversion, old$date <- as.Date(old$date), written before anything touches the column; with read_csv() the conversion has already happened at import.
There are two smaller differences. read.csv() returns int for whole-number columns where read_csv() returns dbl, and before R 4.0.0 it converted character columns into factors, the historical default described in Section 3.3. It is also slower on large files, though at 345 rows the difference is not perceptible.
Both readers load the file. This book uses read_csv() because it reports the column types it assigned, and read.csv() reports nothing.

title: 4  Reading the epidemic in
text:
4.4 Pinning the types
Guessing is convenient when exploring a new file and less suitable for a script that runs every month. readr guesses from the first 1,000 rows by default, so a column that is numeric for a thousand rows and contains the word pending on row 1,500 will be guessed wrong. When the following month’s file differs, the guess differs with it, and the code produces different numbers without reporting the change.
The remedy is to state the types. cols() lets you name the ones that matter and set a fallback for the rest:

covid_pinned <- read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols(
    administrative_area_level_1 = col_character(),
    date                        = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    .default                    = col_double()
  )
)
dim(covid_pinned)
#> [1] 345  13

No specification message appears this time, because there was nothing to guess. The quickest way to write one of these is to read the file once, run spec(), and paste the output into the script as the col_types argument. The import then either matches the stated specification or reports where it does not.
For example, state that every column is numeric, including the two that are not:

bad <- read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_double())
)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, call `problems()` on your data frame for details,
#> e.g.:
#>   dat <- vroom(...)
#>   problems(dat)

That produces a warning rather than an error, and the data still loads, with NA wherever a value could not be parsed. problems() tells you exactly which cells failed:

head(problems(bad))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>     row   col expected actual     file 
#>   <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>      <chr>
#> 1     2     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 2     2     4 a double 2020-01-22 ""   
#> 3     3     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 4     3     4 a double 2020-01-23 ""   
#> 5     4     1 a double Singapore  ""   
#> 6     4     4 a double 2020-01-24 ""

The first failure is at row 2, column 1, where a double was expected and the value Singapore was found. Two columns times 345 rows is 690 failures here. When a real import produces a handful of failures rather than hundreds, those few rows are usually the ones to inspect: typically a note typed into a numeric field.
When you only need part of a wide file, cols_only() reads the named columns and skips the rest, which on a large file saves both time and memory:

read_csv(
  here("data", "sg_covid_data.csv"),
  col_types = cols_only(
    date      = col_date(),
    confirmed = col_double(),
    deaths    = col_double()
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 345 × 3
#>    confirmed deaths date      
#>        <dbl>  <dbl> <date>    
#>  1         0     NA 2020-01-22
#>  2         1     NA 2020-01-23
#>  3         3     NA 2020-01-24
#>  4         3     NA 2020-01-25
#>  5         4     NA 2020-01-26
#>  6         5     NA 2020-01-27
#>  7         7     NA 2020-01-28
#>  8         7     NA 2020-01-29
#>  9        10     NA 2020-01-30
#> 10        13     NA 2020-01-31
#> # ℹ 335 more rows

The columns come back in the order they appear in the file, not the order you listed them, which matters if any later code indexes columns by position.

4.4.1 Other formats
Use read_tsv() for tab-separated files, read_delim() when the separator has to be named explicitly, readxl::read_excel() for .xlsx files, which takes a sheet argument, and the haven package for Stata, SPSS and SAS files, which are common in public health. All of them return tibbles, and haven retains the variable labels that survey datasets carry.

title: 4  Reading the epidemic in
text:
4.5 Looking at what you loaded
glimpse() is the first thing to run after any import. It transposes the usual view: one line per column, running across the page, so a 13-column table fits on a screen.

glimpse(covid)
#> Rows: 345
#> Columns: 13
#> $ administrative_area_level_1                        <chr> "Singapore", "Singa…
#> $ confirmed                                          <dbl> 0, 1, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7…
#> $ deaths                                             <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ date                                               <date> 2020-01-22, 2020-0…
#> $ stringency_index                                   <dbl> 19.44, 25.00, 25.00…
#> $ government_response_index                          <dbl> 19.27, 24.48, 24.48…
#> $ containment_health_index                           <dbl> 22.02, 27.98, 27.98…
#> $ retail_and_recreation_percent_change_from_baseline <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ grocery_and_pharmacy_percent_change_from_baseline  <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ parks_percent_change_from_baseline                 <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ transit_stations_percent_change_from_baseline      <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ workplaces_percent_change_from_baseline            <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
#> $ residential_percent_change_from_baseline           <dbl> NA, NA, NA, NA, NA,…
